articles.title_orig: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
articles.title_zh: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.
The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.
"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."
The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."
Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

articles.title_orig: China’s Huawei Convicted in U.S. Over Bank Fraud, Iran Ties
articles.title_zh: China’s Huawei Convicted in U.S. Over Bank Fraud, Iran Ties
articles.content_orig:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings.
It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations.
The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S.
The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.
“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said .
James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).
Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.
Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement . “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig speaks to reporters outside federal court in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Nov. 24, 2026. Larry Neumeister—AP
Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.
Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.
The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.
The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.
The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.
The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China .
Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.
The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.
Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.
The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.
Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October

articles.title_orig: Asian Stocks to Slide as AI Trade Doubts Resurface: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks to Slide as AI Trade Doubts Resurface: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Asian stock markets have fallen sharply as doubts continue to swirl over the AI boom, reversing a rally led by Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia.
South Korea’s stock market led the sell-off, with the Kospi plunging 6.2 percent.
Taiwan’s Taiex closed down 4.8 percent, after earlier falling more than 8 percent.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 percent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index shed morning gains to finish 1.1 percent in the red.
Tech stocks linked to the AI trade suffered some of the steepest losses.
In Japan, semiconductor equipment makers Tokyo Electron and Advantest dived 12.5 percent and 12.9 percent, respectively.
South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the top two global memory chip makers, sank 9.9 percent and 11.1 percent, respectively.
In Taiwan, Apple supplier Hon Hai Precision Industry, also known as Foxconn, slid 8.8 percent, while top contract chip maker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) closed down 3.6 percent.
The retreat comes after Asian markets surged on Tuesday following Huang’s surprise reinstatement at the helm of chip giant Nvidia after an intervention by US President Donald Trump.
Nvidia’s reappointment of Huang, who resigned amid claims he was romantically involved with a woman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, sent the chip giant’s New York-listed shares 31.5 percent higher on Monday, the largest single-day gain in US stock market history.
Wall Street saw modest losses on Tuesday after the previous session’s buying spree, with the S&P 500 falling 0.5 percent and the Nasdaq composite down 1.5 percent.
Markets have seen wild swings over the past month amid the Nvidia scandal and expectations that Democrats in Washington, DC, will push for greater regulation of AI following their sweeping victories in the US midterm elections.
Those headwinds have added to existing concerns that tech firms may not be able to sustain their multitrillion-dollar investments underpinning the AI boom.
Big Tech’s debt-fuelled splurge has stirred intense debate about whether it is investing in a future gold mine or a massive stock market bubble.
Global AI-related investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

articles.title_orig: China space station receives Pakistani astronaut on 'historic mission'
articles.title_zh: China space station receives Pakistani astronaut on 'historic mission'
articles.content_orig:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station .
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.
Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23 , which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

articles.title_zh: China, US Hold First Agricultural Working Group Meeting
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

The Solomon Islands said Wednesday it won’t allow foreign military bases on its soil, calming worries among the U.S. and allies that the country was slipping into China’s orbit and that Beijing could open a military outpost there.
The nation of more than 800,000 people, stretched out across about 1,000 islands northeast of Australia , made the pledge in a new treaty it signed with Australia, a U.S. ally. Australia has signed several similar treaties with Pacific island states over the past two years, curbing Beijing’s efforts to increase its influence in the region.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Alice Huang-linked firms listed $270 million in AI servers in China, records show
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Alice Huang-linked firms listed $270 million in AI servers in China, records show
articles.content_orig:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title_orig: Trump Says He’s Open To Pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—Who Reportedly Still Holds Security Clearance
articles.title_zh: Trump Says He’s Open To Pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—Who Reportedly Still Holds Security Clearance
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump told The Post in an exclusive interview that he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should “tell the truth” to Congress when he testifies next week .
Trump, who pressured the company’s board to take Huang back, took a victory lap after Nvidia’s stock surged Monday — inspecting the latest numbers at the Resolute Desk during the interview and noting the price ticked up in the afternoon, partially reversing a slump earlier Tuesday.
“That’s not bad, went down a couple of points,” Trump commented while reviewing the numbers. “It really picked up at the end.”
Huang doesn’t need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added.
“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said.
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”
Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes , Trump said, “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress blasted the reinstatement of Huang before getting answers on whether he was a national security threat or violated export controls on shipping chips to communist China.
Angry lawmakers previewed a tough grilling of Huang with Louisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy predicting Huang will plead the Fifth to avoid self-incrimination amid potential criminal prosecution.
Trump said that he hadn’t learned granular details of additional affairs that Huang admitted to before being restored as CEO — after the firestorm over his tryst with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (no relation) and at least two company employees.
The president said, however, that it’s his understanding that Huang wasn’t sleeping with any other women with questionable links to Beijing.
“No, not from what I understand. I didn’t really get into it very much, to be honest with you. But no, from what I understand, no,” Trump replied.
He also said he didn’t know precisely how many affairs Huang fessed up to as part of his restoration.
“I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex,” Trump joked.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
The president said that Nvidia’s success was essential to the US retaining an edge in artificial intelligence — and that he’s even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed over 10% of its value last year.
“I thought about it. I said, ‘You know, maybe I should do it,’ but I didn’t bring it up at this point. It’s probably not too late,” Trump said.
The president said he intervened to restore Huang, including by giving assurances that he faced no issues from the executive branch, because if Nvidia picked “the wrong person” to replace Huang, “that would be a terrible thing for our country in many ways.”

articles.title_orig: Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants
articles.title_zh: Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has continued its attacks on Russian oil refineries despite requests from US President Donald Trump to withhold them, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said while threatening retaliation.
Putin made the threat on Tuesday, after Kyiv said it would stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow did the same.
Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was responsible for Saturday’s drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. One crew member was injured.
The Ukrainian leader told Bloomberg in an interview that the vessel, Sparta II, had been a legitimate target for his military as it was carrying weapons.
Ukrainian attacks on fuel installations subsided after Trump’s mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire in the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But they picked up again in late October.
“We see that the Kyiv regime continues to attack our refining facilities, despite the US president’s appeal and direct request to refrain from such attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are ignoring this advice,” Putin told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin.
“In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable.”
He also told the meeting that he wanted additional security measures for energy facilities.
According to estimates from two industry sources cited by the Reuters news agency, Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October.
Several Russian regions have introduced restrictions on retail sales of petrol and diesel following a renewed spate of Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries, according to local media and authorities.
Putin said that while the situation on the domestic fuel market remained difficult, petrol prices have stabilised after they peaked in October.
Elsewhere, Poland on Tuesday accused Moscow of deliberately violating its airspace when a Russian surveillance drone briefly crossed the border.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.
Moscow on Monday accused Estonia, a NATO and European Union member state, of a range of hostile actions “on the verge of triggering open war”, after Estonia announced the closure of its land border.
In other incidents, Warsaw said three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, and a Russian cargo ship with links to the military was hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday in an attack claimed by Ukraine.
On Sunday, Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette in a Libyan port using maritime drones. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the drone attack was a legitimate act of self-defence, following criticism from Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli.
Additionally, British security officials on Tuesday warned United Kingdom companies providing “material support” for Ukrainian armed forces to brace for Russian sabotage attempts.
Meanwhile, a Russian attack killed two people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia overnight, Governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Tuesday.
Forty people, including four children, were wounded in the assault, Semikin added. Images and a video on his Telegram account showed a damaged apartment building with its windows blown out and rubble on the ground.
The Interfax news agency, citing Russia’s Defence Ministry, said on Tuesday that the Russian military hit drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine’s Sumy region, also killing a number of servicemen.

articles.title_orig: Trump Accounts hit major milestone as family contributions surpass $1 billion
articles.title_zh: Trump Accounts hit major milestone as family contributions surpass $1 billion
articles.content_orig:
Former Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender analyzes the potential expansion of Trump accounts for adults. He also weighs in on the challenges China's domestic economy is facing.
Contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts have surpassed $1 billion, marking a major milestone for the children's investment program as Americans prepare for the holiday season.
More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual Trump Accounts — investment accounts established for children under 18 — surpassing $1 billion in personal contributions, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business.
Combined with philanthropic gifts and the federal government's $1,000 seed contributions for eligible children, total assets deposited in Trump Accounts have now surpassed $9 billion.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent praised the milestone Tuesday, saying Americans were increasingly taking advantage of the program to invest in children's financial futures.
HOUSE DEM TARGETS 4 COMPANIES IN PROBE INTO TRUMP JR-LINKED 1789 CAPITAL
President Donald Trump speaks during the Trump Accounts Launch Summit in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Jan. 28, 2026. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," Bessent said in a statement.
"President Trump wanted to make it especially easy to contribute to Trump Accounts, and friends and families across the country are seizing that opportunity to help the next generation build wealth from day one," he continued.
Bessent added that each contribution helps bring the promise of long-term financial security within reach of American children.
He also said that President Donald Trump had joined millions of Americans making personal contributions to individual accounts.
"This week, the President himself joined the millions of Americans who have made personal donations to individual Trump Accounts," Bessent said.
BANK OF AMERICA CEO HONORED AT $32M FUNDRAISING EVENT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent praised the milestone after contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts surpassed $1 billion nationwide. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images)
Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government.
While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions.
With the holiday season approaching, friends and relatives can contribute directly to a child's Trump Account once it has been claimed.
According to Treasury, contributors can use a QR code generated through the child's Trump Accounts app to make deposits.
TOP TRUMP CRYPTO MEME COIN HOLDERS AWARDED WITH EXCLUSIVE DINNER EVENT
President Donald Trump's children's investment account program surpassed $1 billion in contributions from friends and family members, according to the Treasury Department. (Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Family members and friends can contribute up to a combined $5,000 per year to each account, while employers can contribute up to $2,500 annually, subject to the overall $5,000 limit.
The latest milestone follows the Treasury Department's announcement last month that approximately 70 million Trump Accounts had been established for eligible children.
Major philanthropic donors have also pledged support to the program, including Michael and Susan Dell, who pledged approximately $6.25 billion to provide $250 to 25 million eligible children.

President Donald Trump displays a signed document alongside Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano in the Oval Office, pictured next to a graphic of the new $1,000 Trump Account notice being sent to parents of newborns. (Social Security Administration)
Parents and guardians can claim their children's accounts through the official Trump Accounts app. Additional information is available at TrumpAccounts.gov.

articles.title_orig: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali into space
articles.title_zh: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali into space
articles.content_orig:
China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.
Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.
Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a triumphant return to the semiconductor giant in an all-hands meeting Tuesday morning, apologizing to staff for his conduct during his previous stint at the company’s helm and vowing to do better this time around.
No company has impacted the world as deeply or profoundly as Nvidia, Huang said, according to an Nvidia employee who attended the meeting. Huang called the company’s story the most interesting in the world.
According to the individual, Huang expressed contrition for his past behavior and was adamant that employees should follow the company’s code of conduct. The AI hardware leader resigned from the company on Nov. 12 amid mounting scrutiny about alleged romantic relationships with subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence officials, Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
He also said that he has been regularly attending therapy and that he had been deeply embarrassed about recent events, the source said. The CEO was met with an overwhelmingly positive reception, even receiving a standing ovation, according to the source.
Huang’s return marked a nearly unprecedented case of corporate whiplash. After a wave of reports emerged stating that Huang had been involved in extramarital relationships — potentially with someone accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset — Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a letter sent to Nvidia employees and shared online on Nov. 8.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang wrote at the time. “I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”
Huang issued a personal statement on Nov. 17, expressing remorse but professing his admiration for and dedication to Nvidia. Huang founded the semiconductor designer in 1993 and grew it into what was once the world’s most valuable company.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote in that statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Less than a week later, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang would return to the company — backed by “input from senior levels of the United States government” that essentially guaranteed “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Huang said in Tuesday’s meeting that President Donald Trump supported the company. “President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said, according to the Nvidia employee.
Huang said that Nvidia was an apolitical company. Huang added that he returned as CEO because the board — and not the government — had wanted him to be reinstalled.
The meeting, which kicked off around 9:30 a.m., lasted around an hour, according to the source, who added that Huang exited to the Foo Fighters’ song “Times Like These.”
Jean Lee reports with NBC News’ Social Newsgathering team in Los Angeles. She previously reported for the NBC News investigative unit.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: TSA anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week
articles.title_zh: TSA anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week
articles.content_orig:
The Transportation Security Administration expects to screen roughly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between Tuesday and next Monday, projecting more than 3 million travelers on the Sunday after Thanksgiving alone.
The Transportation Security Administration announced on Tuesday that it anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week, vowing to help families reach their loved ones for the holiday "as safely and securely as possible."
The agency said it expects to screen about 17.6 million air travelers across the country between Nov. 24 and 29, including more than 3 million passengers at U.S. airports on the Sunday after Thanksgiving.
"TSA is prepared to handle the increased passenger volumes expected during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period while maintaining our focus on security," TSA Administrator David Cummins said in a statement. "I am grateful to the TSA employees who will work throughout the holiday to help ensure the traveling public reaches their destinations safely. A little preparation by passengers can help make the screening process more efficient for everyone."
The TSA urged people traveling over Thanksgiving week to arrive at the airport at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights.
FAA ISSUES GROUND DELAY AT CHICAGO O'HARE DUE TO 'EQUIPMENT OUTAGE'
The Transportation Security Administration announced on Tuesday that it anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week. (Peter Zay/Anadolu via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Travelers should give themselves extra time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop-off and security screening, the agency said.
"At TSA, our highest priority is security," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. "While our partners at the Federal Aviation Administration and the airlines oversee other aspects of your journey, TSA is responsible for screening everyone safely and securely. DHS is ready to help ensure millions of American families can reach their loved ones as safely and securely as possible over the coming days. I also want to thank our patriotic TSA employees for working tirelessly to deliver on our homeland security mission during this busy holiday season."
The Federal Aviation Administration also predicted the busiest holiday skies in 16 years for Thanksgiving week.
The FAA said there were more than 417,000 forecast flights over a nine-day holiday period. Tuesday was set to be the busiest travel day, with 52,345 flights expected to take off.
For flights home after Thanksgiving, 44,265 flights are scheduled on Saturday, while 50,314 are set for Sunday, the FAA said.
DUFFY SOUNDS ALARM OVER AGING FAA SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE AIR TRAVEL SHUTDOWN
The TSA said travelers should give themselves extra time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop-off and security screening. (REUTERS/Aaron Schwartz / Reuters)
"Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. "The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century."
The agency added that weather conditions could impact flights throughout the week.
On Tuesday, low ceilings were forecast to affect flights along the West Coast. Thunderstorms were possible across Florida and the Gulf Coast on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Rain could affect flights across the Southeast, including Atlanta, on Wednesday before moving into the Mid-Atlantic later in the day. Rain and wind are expected to impact the Northeast on Thanksgiving Day.
The anticipated heavy travel for Thanksgiving week comes after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 due to telecommunications equipment failures, interrupting travel for more than a million travelers during the nearly four-hour delay.
The TSA said it expects to screen more than 3 million passengers at U.S. airports on the Sunday after Thanksgiving. (Erin Hooley/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service / Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO READ MORE ON FOX BUSINESS
The FAA also issued a ground stop on Tuesday afternoon for regional flights arriving at Chicago-O'Hare due to an equipment failure with the airport's runway surface radar. The ground stop was lifted after about an hour, and a subsequent ground delay was canceled about an hour after that.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Tuesday that Americans "can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time."
"As millions of Americans prepare to hit the road or take to the skies to spend the holiday season with their loved ones, the Trump Administration's message is clear: your safety is our number one priority. From standing up a Tiger Team to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we’ve taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancelations," he said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.title_zh: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine .
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.
Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.
North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.
Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.
“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.
It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.
The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.
Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.
The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.
In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”
Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.
During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

articles.title_orig: Israel kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.title_zh: Israel kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.
Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces .
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.
Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.
Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.
Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.
Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.
The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".
Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.
Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.
Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.
Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.
“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.
It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.
The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.
Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.
The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.
In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”
Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.
During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks Is Said to Engage Banks for Sale of Japan Business
articles.title_zh: Starbucks Is Said to Engage Banks for Sale of Japan Business
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks Corp. (SBUX) has enlisted Citigroup (C) and Morgan Stanley (MS) to prepare a possible sale of its Japan business, a market that could fetch several billion dollars and ranks among the coffee chain's largest outside the United States.
The Seattle-based company has begun testing appetite among strategic and financial investors, and a formal process could get underway as soon as this year, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg News. The deliberations are preliminary and may not produce a transaction.
A Starbucks spokesperson said the company routinely evaluates structures that best serve customers and create value for shareholders, adding that the Japanese operation remains strong after more than three decades in the country. The company does not break out Japan revenue on its own; Japan, Canada and the U.K. together accounted for roughly 72% of net revenue outside the U.S. and China in fiscal 2026.
Starbucks operates about 2,000 coffeehouses in Japan, a footprint smaller than its roughly 8,000 stores in mainland China but still one of its most established company-operated markets. The Japan business has faced persistent pressure from local chains and rising operating costs.
Note: Store counts are approximate and based on reported figures.
The move follows a template Starbucks set with its China business. In November 2025 the company agreed to form a joint venture with Chinese private equity firm Boyu Capital, which took a stake of up to 60% in the mainland retail operation on a cash-free, debt-free enterprise value of about $4 billion. Starbucks retained 40%, kept ownership of the brand and intellectual property, and said at the time the total value of the China retail business would exceed $13 billion. The deal closed in March 2026, converting some 8,000 stores to a licensed model.
That transaction came after years of aggressive price competition in China, where domestic chains such as Luckin and Cotti pushed heavily discounted coffee. Japan presents a different set of challenges, but the strategic logic is similar: ceding a measure of control in a mature market to local capital in exchange for capital returns and greater operational flexibility.
Reuters reported in September that Starbucks was weighing the sale of a majority stake in Japan in a deal that could value the business at about $3 billion, and the company had already held early talks with banks at that time.
For investors, the Japan review signals that Chief Executive Brian Niccol's turnaround plan extends beyond U.S. store operations into portfolio reshaping. Proceeds from any deal would give Starbucks room to pay down debt, fund share buybacks or reinvest in its home market, where traffic recovery has been the central concern. A sale or joint venture would also shift a slice of earnings off the company's balance sheet, reducing exposure to yen fluctuations and Japanese labor costs.
The structure matters for valuation. A minority-stake sale or joint venture, following the China precedent, would let Starbucks book a gain while retaining brand royalties and long-term upside. A full exit would raise more cash upfront but surrender a market the company has cultivated since opening its first Japanese store in 1996.
Attention now turns to whether Canada and the U.K., the other mature markets grouped with Japan in Starbucks' international reporting, will face similar reviews as the company continues to assess the best structure for each region.

articles.title_orig: Ten hostages released in standoff with gunmen at Colombia supermarket
articles.title_zh: Ten hostages released in standoff with gunmen at Colombia supermarket
articles.content_orig:
Colombia’s president has said all 20 people held hostage by armed men in a supermarket in the city of Cartagena have been rescued. Security forces stormed the supermarket early on Wednesday, ending a daylong siege.
“In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued,” President Abelardo de la Espriella said early on Wednesday, adding that one captor was killed.
The hostage incident came after an unsuccessful attempt to rob an armoured vehicle, the Colombian police said.
De la Espriella said the robbers sought refuge in a nearby store after security camera operators alerted police to the attempted robbery.
Images from the Reuters news agency showed heavily armed police and military personnel outside the Exito supermarket in the neighbourhood of La Castellana.
Unverified footage shared on social media appeared to show people inside the supermarket kneeling against the windows with their hands bound.
The incident comes as de la Espriella, who campaigned on a promise to crack down on crime, faces a series of high-profile incidents that underscore the country’s ongoing issues with violence and insecurity.
The president made his remarks from the city of Villavicencio, where he had travelled in the aftermath of a recent car bombing the government attributed to an armed group.
Politicians have already weighed in on the incident, blaming failures in de la Espriella’s security platform.
“The root cause of this violence is the impoverishment of the population, brought about by the collapse of the tourism sector,” former President Gustavo Petro wrote on social media.
“Destroying tourism — through state-sanctioned violence, such as the desecration of corpses, and by making death the central theme of presidential discourse — has dismantled a dynamic source of wealth that once attracted 7 million foreign tourists,” he added.
De la Espriella beat Petro’s handpicked successor, Senator Ivan Cepeda, in a June 21 run-off election.

articles.title_orig: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.title_zh: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.content_orig:
Giorgia Meloni has a Ukraine problem.
With a national Italian election possible as early as this spring, Kyiv’s weekend strikes on a Russian warship and cargo vessel in Libya risk sparking a backlash in Rome — a Kyiv ally that also has traditionally close ties with the North African country.
“If this is a continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine just a few hundred kilometers from Italy, this is worrying, especially because we work for the stability of Libya,” said Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, who added that Rome had not been informed ahead of time about the attack.
The Italian foreign ministry said Tajani spoke with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday.
"The Minister reiterated to his Ukrainian counterpart how vital it is for Italy to continue working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading to the Mediterranean as well," the ministry said in a statement . For Italy, "it is essential to respect Libya’s sovereignty and to continue working towards the country’s stability, unity and sovereignty."
Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, a pro-Kremlin junior partner in Meloni’s governing coalition, that opposes further military aid to Ukraine said that “it wouldn't make sense” if military support provided to Ukraine “ends up making wars and sinking ships around the world.”
Kyiv defended its right to strike Russian vessels — even those docked in Benghazi, thousands of kilometers away from the battlefield.
The issue threatens to become a headache for Meloni.
Rome is especially concerned about destabilizing Libya, a former Italian colony, fearing that if the politically fragile country collapses into disorder again, it could spark a migration wave across the Mediterranean.
Russia and its allies in Libya could use migration as a weapon against the country, said Arturo Varvelli, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.
“For Italy, Libya is the most important foreign policy dossier because everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy,” said Lia Quartapelle, a center-left Democratic Party lawmaker and vice chair of the Foreign and European Affairs Committee of Italy’s parliament.
Meloni's strong backing for Ukraine puts her at odds with part of her coalition, as well as with large parts of the political opposition.
This summer, former Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte, leader of the populist 5Star Movement, a key opposition party, set off a political firestorm by questioning further military aid to Ukraine if the center-left wins the next election.
The far-right opposition National Future Party, led by former Gen. Roberto Vannacci, also opposes military aid to Ukraine.
The public is also skeptical. Italians are the least likely to support Ukraine among major Western European countries, with a YouGov survey earlier this year finding that only 32% of Italians care if it wins against Russia.
For Meloni, "it’s a difficult match to handle," said pollster Lorenzo Pregliasco. "We [Italians] are afraid to take sides; we tend to be wary of conflict and of any Italian involvement in any conflict whatsoever."
That national caution has made Italy a relatively small donor to Ukraine — giving far less than countries like Germany or Nordic nations. Italy has provided around €3 billion in military aid, boosted by a new €800 million package.
Although there is worry about blowback, military giving "is unlikely to be affected in a meaningful way by the Ukrainian attacks," said Alessandro Marrone, who leads the defense, security and space program at Rome’s Istituto Affari Internazionali.
And it's not just Italy that is worried about a widening war in the Mediterranean.
“Greece’s government is concerned that the war in Ukraine could open another front in the eastern Mediterranean and is planning to have discussions on the issue with like-minded partners in the near future,” a senior Greek government official said.
Despite the turmoil in Rome and Athens, Kyiv stands by its decision to attack Russian ships.
“Ukraine is defending itself against the armed aggression of the Russian Federation. Our actions constitute the exercise of the inherent right to self-defense," Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters on Tuesday.
"Ukraine has the full right to strike the aggressor’s legitimate military targets. These include Russian warships, cargo vessels transporting military equipment and resources, and tankers belonging to the shadow fleet that sustain Russia’s war machine," he said. "Ukraine is not dragging anyone into the war, nor is it exporting the conflict elsewhere."
There is another risk for Meloni: that Ukraine ends up showing the lack of an Italian strategy in Libya to deal with the Russian presence there, said Varvelli, the ECFR researcher. The Russian naval vessel was sunk in the eastern Libyan port of Benghazi, controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army is allied with Moscow.
"The Ukrainians are simply bringing to light the significant Russian presence in Libya, which consists of six bases and between 1,000 and 1,500 personnel," he said, warning that Italy is “purely reactive” to what is happening in the country.
Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv and Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting from Athens.

articles.title_orig: Trump Weighs Fresh Tariffs on India and China: What is Behind the US Trade Investigation?
articles.title_zh: Trump Weighs Fresh Tariffs on India and China: What is Behind the US Trade Investigation?
articles.content_orig:
For a minute there, it seemed like someone in the Trump administration might actually be willing to stand up to China.
For about a week and a half, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia over the potential risks its co-founder Jensen Huang 's affairs posed to national security. Bessent was giving voice to China hawks who had felt sidelined by the Trump administration's willingness to sell artificial intelligence chips to  China.
They see China's AI program as a major threat, and want to restrain its growth by cutting off the supply of advanced chips to China. The resignation of Huang, who pressed the Trump Administration to allow the exports, seemed to signal that the hawks had found new influence in Washington.
By this weekend, Bessent had softened his public resistance to Huang's reinstatement. That came just in time for Nvidia's board to reappoint Huang as CEO at President Donald Trump 's urging.
Whether any real damage was done to national security isn't clear. But it is safe to say that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress won't take Trump at his word when he said on CNBC Monday that the Department of Justice "did a pretty good investigation" that exonerated Huang.
Congress will look deeply into the worries Bessent himself raised about Huang's acknowledged romantic relationship with a woman The New York Times and others have reported was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from top U.S. officials and had concluded his return wasn't a national security risk.
A top concern is whether China was able to use the affair to help divert Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence chips toward helping its military. Bessent in a Nov. 13 interview with CNBC outlined the stakes.
"Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the — it hurts our great companies and in the AI race it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Bessent said that his department and others had wanted to blacklist Megaspeed, the company previously run by Alice Huang, Jensen Huang's paramour. But "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The Commerce Department is headed by Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bessent's rival.
Putting Huang back at Nvidia wasn't originally Bessent's preference. He said in a Fox interview on Nov. 15 that the board should "go outside the company" to find a new leader. But by this past weekend, Bessent had apparently gotten on board with Trump's wishes.
"Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent told CBS on Sunday, in trying to explain his apparent policy shift.
Commerce has since taken steps to tighten some restrictions meant to prevent U.S. chips from helping China advance in the AI race.
But there is bipartisan worry about the Nvidia episode. "I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done," Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told The Wall Street Journal . He said Lutnick had not responded to letters he sent saying the administration should be "taking the threats of communist China more seriously."
But Trump has clearly put an upper limit on how aggressively anyone in his administration can push back on China. The president said Monday that he was swayed by the pageantry in his visit to China last week.
Xi "met me at the plane, which is something they've never done, which was a sign," Trump said.
Trump said he felt like he needed to intervene to back Huang because the stock market was plummeting in the wake of Nvidia's troubles — a development he also blamed on Democrats' midterm victory.
"I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election," he said. "If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come." Now, its stock performance will be "unbelievable."
Bessent on Sunday played down the market risks. The company "continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide," he told CBS.
Lutnick has embraced Trump's transactional urges. He has backed deals in which the U.S. takes equity stakes in companies such as Intel, saying the taxpayer deserves some of the upside.
Lutnick in January said he had heard Huang pitch Trump on allowing Nvidia to sell its relatively more advanced H200 chips into China.
"There are strong — two sides. We shouldn't sell them any or we should sell them." Where does he stand? "Right in the middle," Lutnick told Bloomberg . Trump decided to go ahead with the deal.
Bessent has said he is "neither a hawk nor a dove" on China, and is simply trying to manage the ultra-sensitive relationship between the world's two biggest economies. But the upshot of the Huang affair seems to be that Bessent wasn't able to sway the president on a matter that seemed cut-and-dried just days ago.
Lutnick, meanwhile, is riding high.
Trump said he discussed whether Huang should return to Nvidia with Lutnick, Bessent and Vice President JD Vance. "Howard Lutnick was very good. Very, he's very professional," Trump said on CNBC Monday.
"I call them the opposites, Scott and Howard," Trump added, before declaring them "both good."
