articles.title_orig: A leak from Russia’s federal statistics agency made it possible to estimate the country’s military death toll in the war against Ukraine. What else did it reveal?
articles.title_zh: A leak from Russia’s federal statistics agency made it possible to estimate the country’s military death toll in the war against Ukraine. What else did it reveal?
articles.content_orig:
At least 700,000 Russian service members have died in the war against Ukraine. Journalists from Meduza and Mediazona reached that figure using data that the hacker groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow obtained when they broke into a database belonging to Rosstat, Russia’s federal statistics agency. It’s the first estimate to include service members listed as missing. Other researchers have also studied the hacked Rosstat data. Here’s what they found.
Journalists who studied the hacked Rosstat database produced different estimates of Russia’s losses in the war against Ukraine. The outlets reported two kinds of figures:
Because the share of service members listed as missing has grown rapidly in recent years, the two types of estimates can differ widely.
The outlets arrived at roughly the same counts for deaths already on record. Meduza and Mediazona estimated that 490,000 Russian service members died in the war against Ukraine from its start to the beginning of fall 2026. Novaya Gazeta Europe gave the same estimate . iStories (Vazhnye Istorii) said it could confidently classify 474,000 deaths in Rosstat’s records as military deaths. The count rose to more than 499,000 when it included less clear-cut cases. Proekt counted 474,000 war-related deaths.
The estimates varied because the outlets classified different categories of causes of death as directly related to the war and handled records with missing causes, circumstances, or other information differently. You can read more about these categories and how we added them up in our article .
Estimates of the total death toll varied more because they had to account for deaths still to be registered. Researchers have to use a model to make these estimates, and choosing which one to use is a judgment call.
iStories estimated the death toll at 611,000, factoring in deaths that had yet to be registered. The outlet noted that its estimate excluded everyone declared dead by a court. More than 40,000 registered deaths already fall into that category, and the number grows each year. In its latest update, Novaya Gazeta Europe estimated 670,000 deaths by projecting how quickly deaths would be registered based on earlier records. As far as we can tell, the outlet did not account for several shifts in that rate caused by changes that simplified the procedure for declaring someone dead.
Meduza estimates that more than 720,000 Russian service members had died by the start of fall 2026, including those whose deaths had yet to be registered. Our model is based on the Berkson-Gage cure model from epidemiology. It draws on death records from the Rosstat leak, missing-person notices that relatives posted over time, the national probate registry, and lists naming those who died. It also accounts for the three ways a death can be registered, each with its own delays. Registration can be based on a medical report, an official death certificate, or a court ruling. The share of deaths registered through each route also changes over time. Using multiple sources and modeling each registration method separately help eliminate calendar effects and make the model’s predictions more accurate. You can read more about these calculations in Meduza’s article.
Explosions and shrapnel accounted for 92% of Russian military deaths in the combat zone, iStories also noted . Gunshot wounds accounted for just 1.3%. Agentstvo calculated that less than 7% of service members’ deaths were due to noncombat causes . The most common noncombat causes are chronic heart disease and cardiomyopathy (more than 2,000 cases) and acute ischemic conditions and heart attacks (more than 1,000 cases). Others include traffic accidents, poisonings and overdoses, and suicides.
After analyzing the leaked Rosstat data, Agentstvo concluded that more than 1,000 people died in the war against Ukraine shortly after signing military contracts with the Defense Ministry at age 18 or 19. Agentstvo said the count might mistakenly include young people killed in shelling. For men ages 20 to 39, the war has become the leading cause of death, Agentstvo calculated.
Russia captured about 1,000 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in 2026, including seven cities and towns, Novaya Gazeta Europe estimated . Rosstat’s database already records more than 55,000 Russian military deaths since the start of the year. Novaya Gazeta Europe estimated that 120 to 180 Russian troops died for every square kilometer Russia captured. The outlet said that figure was two to three times as high as a year earlier and the highest since at least 2023, when Ukraine was carrying out a counteroffensive and Russia was losing territory.
iStories found that in late 2022, Rosstat’s regional office in Rostov-on-Don reported a sharp increase in deaths related to military action. The city is home to the 522nd Center for the Reception, Processing, and Dispatch of the Dead, which handles the bodies of soldiers killed in the war against Ukraine. The Justice Ministry developed an algorithm specifically to reassign death records. From then on, military deaths were counted in the regions where service members had lived instead of where their deaths were registered. The change drew complaints from officials in regions where recorded death rates rose.
Official documents list “myocardial degeneration” (damage to heart muscle tissue) and pulmonary edema as the cause of Ukrainian journalist Viktoria Roshchyna’s death, BBC News Russian , Verstka , and iStories found. The first record of Roshchyna’s death appeared in Rosstat’s database in December 2024. It initially gave her date of death as December 19, 2024, but the date was later corrected to September 19 of that year. The records first specified a cause of death in February 2025, a few days before Roshchyna’s body was handed over to Ukraine.
Suicides fell overall in Russia in 2025, but iStories found they rose nearly 12% among 10- to 19-year-olds. The biggest increase in that age group was among girls ages 15 to 19, at 26%. Suicides also rose 11% among women ages 20 to 29. The total number of registered suicides in Russia in 2025 fell to a record low of 9,600. iStories linked the record-low total to the war, noting that men account for 80% of suicides on average and that some men who might have taken their own lives died in the war.
At least 1,850 women and girls were killed at home from 2023 to 2026. Another 12,000 died at home from “injuries of undetermined intent.” The classification means the death resulted from an external cause, but the records do not establish whether it was a homicide, a suicide, or an accident. Verstka believes this category includes victims of domestic violence. iStories suggests that suicides are also classified this way to lower the official suicide figures.
Of 34 high-profile deaths of businesspeople and officials, only 10 were recorded in Rosstat’s databases as suicides. Rosstat listed the manner of death as “undetermined” in the remaining cases, including the suicide of former Kursk Governor Roman Starovoit. According to the official account, Starovoit shot himself with a pistol he had received as an award.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected] .
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

articles.title_orig: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
articles.title_zh: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Accurately predicting protein structures has been the preserve of specialist AI tools like AlphaFold — but now general-purpose models are catching up. Credit: EMBL-EBI (CC0)
Earlier this month, Xinming Tu set out to test what artificial-intelligence models know about proteins. Tu, a researcher at an AI biology company called Phylo in South San Francisco, California, asked large language models (LLMs) from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to predict the sequences of obscure bacterial proteins.
He left the analysis to run overnight and woke up shocked at the results. The latest versions of Anthropic’s Claude models had outperformed other LLMs — but also specialized ‘protein language models’, which are trained on vast troves of sequence data and specially designed for such tasks.
Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins
Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins
When Tu and Leo Chen, a computational biologist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, shared the results in a 16 November blogpost , it set off a frenzy among computational biologists to see what other protein biology LLMs such as Claude could do. For instance, Tu and Chen and others have found it could perform a key step in protein-structure prediction.
And on 24 November, OpenAI announced that its latest language models had successfully designed new proteins, some of which behaved as expected when made and tested in the lab. The results hint that the latest LLMs might be gaining a sophisticated understanding of protein biology.
The research has kicked off a debate over the future of biological AI . Some scientists predict that ‘general purpose’ models such as Claude and ChatGPT will eventually outperform specialist tools such as AlphaFold at tasks including protein structure prediction and design.
“We want to see a world where a scientist can just describe in natural language what they want a ChatGPT model to do, and the model can just be infinitely flexible and design exactly what the person wants,” says Joy Jiao, who leads life-sciences research at OpenAI in San Francisco, California.
But some researchers question the extent to which LLMs are learning underlying lessons in protein biology. They suggest that some of their abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data.
The release of AlphaFold2, Google DeepMind’s blockbuster protein-structure-prediction AI , in 2020 launched a revolution in biological AI. There is now a vast ecosystem of software — much of it open source — for modelling different properties of proteins, such as how they interact with possible drugs, and for designing new proteins.
Researchers have begun using LLMs to orchestrate these specialist models, but it has mostly been as a time-saving measure, says Martin Pačesa, a structural biologist at the University of Zurich. “In most cases, a specialist will always perform better than a generalist for a given task,” he says.
Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI
Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI
To see if an LLM could stand in for specialist protein-design tools, Jiao and her colleagues asked an OpenAI model called GPT-6.2 to design 3D protein structures capable of binding to five different biological targets, including proteins implicated in cancer and immune disorders. After the LLMs generated the designs, the researchers used a specialist AI tool to determine a corresponding genetic sequence. Lab experiments confirmed that around 11% of designs were able to bind their target.
In other experiments, the OpenAI team showed that its LLMs could design protein sequences, redesign existing antibodies, and other tasks typically performed by specialist tools. In some cases, the LLM performed as well as some specialist tools, and in others, such as predicting the 3D structure of proteins, it was far off. OpenAI researchers describe the work in a blogpost and technical paper .
Jiao emphasizes that the work is a proof of principle, and that specialized AI tools were still needed for key steps. But Masatoshi Uehara, an OpenAI researcher who was part of the effort, believes that LLMs will only get better at protein biology. “I believe the large language model can technically beat every specialized model in even each capability,” he says.

articles.title_orig: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.title_zh: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.content_orig:
A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.
It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.
Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.
Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps
articles.title_zh: Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps
articles.content_orig:
UPDATED 21:36 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026
Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.
It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.
The company said today that users can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.
However, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant users first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.
Anthropic said people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the company said.
That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s new “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.
In a video posted on X, Anthropic showed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.
You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.
Ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq
— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026
Because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to users, Anthropic said.
As an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic said. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.
In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.
The Install as App feature is available in beta test now to all Claude subscribers, with the exception of HIPAA-compliant organizations and hybrid Claude deployments. Subscribers on Team plans will have the feature enabled by default, while Enterprise subscribers will need an administrator to enable the feature first.
There is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”
That could be a pretty big downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

articles.title_orig: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.title_zh: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: Trump says pardon is always an option for Jensen Huang, and that pleading the Fifth isn’t necessary
articles.title_zh: Trump says pardon is always an option for Jensen Huang, and that pleading the Fifth isn’t necessary
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said that while pardoning Jensen Huang for any potential criminal activity remains an option, he doesn’t think that will be needed for the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO .
“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump told the New York Post in an interview published Tuesday night.
Asked about Huang’s scheduled appearances next week on Capitol Hill, Trump said, “I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people.”
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person,” the president said.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on Trump’s comments. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated he would have told Trump if Huang had been involved in any criminal activity.
“To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.
In Congress, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are preparing to grill Huang over their national security concerns.
A spokesperson for the Republican-led House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement “changes nothing” and that there “are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers.”
Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are expected to sit for transcribed interviews next Tuesday and Wednesday before the House Select Committee on China, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Huang, who has not been charged with a crime, resigned from his post as CEO of the chip giant following reports that he had a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. In a Nov. 8 memo to Nvidia’s staff, he said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Trump worked behind the scenes over the weekend to get Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. That move has been met with bipartisan backlash.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., on Monday raised concerns over Nvidia’s quick reversal to rehire Huang after indicating it wouldn’t.
“His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Ricketts wrote in a post on X.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., wrote that with Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang, “the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”
Cramer and Ricketts are both members of the Senate Banking Committee, where Huang is scheduled to testify in public Dec. 3.
In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social post that the U.S. government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
Similarly, Nvidia’s board said it reached the decision to reinstate Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.content_orig:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11.
The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh.
The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians.
The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis.
Turki al-Maliki , a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh.
He added that authorities were conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack.
This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties.
On Wednesday, Houthi brigadier general Yahya Saree warned on X that the port of Jeddah and all Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will become "targets for our forces," if Riyadh attacks the Yemeni Red Sea port of Hodeidah.
The coalition had asked civilians to evacuate the port "for their safety," on Nov. 20.
Attacks by the rebel Houthis have been escalating on Saudi Arabia, with the group targeting one of Saudi Arabia's oil refineries on Sunday , according to Reuters. The Houthis also launched drone and ballistic missiles against the country's airports, most recently targeting the King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 25 , according to reports.
The new attacks come amid wider strikes by Tehran and Iran-linked forces in the Gulf, with Bahrain also reporting that it was attacked by Iran over the weekend. Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.
"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X.
The ministry later said two people , a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.
— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: See all of Trump’s Nvidia stock trades since January
articles.content_orig:
SALT LAKE CITY — Utah Sen. John Curtis said he agreed with tech CEO Jensen Huang's initial decision to step down from Nvidia and appeared skeptical about Huang's sudden reinstatement this week.
Huang's surprise comeback as head of one of the world's most prominent chip manufacturers was met with bipartisan pushback. Huang initially left the company after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump took credit for Huang's return to Nvidia. But the move prompted skepticism from some in Washington, including Curtis.
"Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk," the Republican senator wrote on X. "I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
He added that Huang's initial decision to leave Nvidia after news of the affair broke was the right call.
"Just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure, the board brought him back while its own independent investigation was still underway," Curtis continued. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed."
Meanwhile, Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, has been quiet on social media about Huang and the controversy surrounding his role at Nvidia. A spokesperson did not immediately respond Tuesday when asked if Lee had any comment on Huang's reinstatement at the tech company.
Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, called for Congress to investigate the situation.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," he wrote on social media. "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that is a customer of Nvidia. The alleged spy Huang had an affair with is a former executive for the company.
During a company-wide meeting Tuesday, Huang apologized to employees for making "some terrible mistakes," according to the New York Times , but he challenged the notion that he was back only because Trump pushed for it.
The president's involvement in the issue has raised questions about Nvidia's independence at a time when many are worried about a race with China to develop artificial general intelligence.
"In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company," Peter Cohan, associate professor of management practice at Babson College in Massachusetts, told the Associated Press . "That's because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it."
Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney also weighed in on the latest AI developments on Tuesday, referring to the reported sales of AI chips to China.
"Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they'd need to get ahead of us," Romney wrote on X. "Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse."
The U.S. Department of Commerce has approved selling more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies this year, including companies with ties to the Chinese military, the New York Times reported last week. On Sunday, before Huang was renamed CEO, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for answers about Nvidia's chip sales to China.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers," he told CBS' "Face the Nation."

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
articles.content_orig:
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing opposition party in a bid to form the next Israeli government following October’s elections .
The Yashar party said on Tuesday that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
After no party managed to secure a 61-seat majority, Israel’s parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming ⁠a government, while Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister despite the October 27 election stripping Netanyahu of his majority.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
The agreement between Eisenkot, whose party won 21 parliament seats, and Lieberman, whose party won seven, was unforeseen since Lieberman has been vocal about his opposition to forming a government with support from Arab parties as well as to a unity government with Netanyahu.
Lieberman had once served as foreign minister under a previous Netanyahu government but has since become a strong critic.
Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners, including Lieberman, hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and ⁠are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his “change bloc” partners and Likud on forming a unity government.
The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot after the Yashar party leader’s talks with Netanyahu’s Likud on a possible unity government.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with Arab parties.

articles.title_orig: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.title_zh: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.content_orig:
Ferrari’s new 296 Challenge Stradale is a badass, 670-horsepower, non-hybrid race car for the road. Want one? It’ll cost you around $307,000 before options.
But if you want to get a little fancier with your new Ferrari, the automaker’s online configurator has plenty of ways to customize the supercar. And some of them are pretty wild. I wasted 30 minutes of my day dialing in my perfect 296 CS.
Let’s start with the most important part: paint. Ferrari offers a whopping 35 colors, split into four categories: Standard, Historical, Classic, and Special. You could go with the classic Rosso Corsa or Giallo Modena, but I'm going with something a little different here: Giallo Ambra, aka fancy orange.
Once you pick your paint, Ferrari lets you choose from a handful of livery options, including upper- and lower-body graphics, wing decals, door numbers, and more. Normally, I'd say a livery is mandatory on a car like this. But the 296 Challenge Stradale looks so damn good in a single color that it really doesn't need one.
Ferrari also lets you turn just about anything into carbon fiber. Front splitter? Carbon fiber. Rear diffuser? Carbon fiber. Even the engine covers? That's right, carbon fiber.
If you really want to go crazy, you can replace all the glass with Lexan, a lightweight polycarbonate that's a little lighter than traditional glass. That should help shave off a few pounds. Ferrari will even let you ditch the Prancing Horse badges on the front fenders entirely or swap the metal logos for painted ones.
Ferrari offers six wheel designs for the 296 CS, ranging from light silver to darker gray and black. You can also customize the wheel bolts, center caps, and more. I'm going with Forged Diamond-Polished wheels and titanium wheel bolts.
Depending on how you plan to use your 296 (primarily on road or track), Ferrari offers both Bridgestone and Pirelli tires. There are even two Pirelli "Color Edition" options with yellow or gray accents. We'll pass on those.
Brake calipers are available in eight different colors, ranging from black and red to yellow and silver.
Most of the interior upgrades are pretty subtle. You can choose floor mats with or without logos, pick from 26 stitching colors (we went with Filo Spec Flash Orange to match the exterior), and customize the lower portion of the dashboard with 22 different colors.
Perhaps the most important choice, though, is the seats. Ferrari offers two options: Racing and "Best Weight," as the automaker calls it. The racing seats appear to be lighter and probably less comfortable, but Ferrari doesn't really divulge any specifics.
There are seven different Alcantara colors available, depending on which seats you choose. You can also customize the seatbelts with six different colors, add a central racing stripe, and choose from additional stitching options.
Like most Ferraris, the 296 CS doesn't have a dedicated center touchscreen. That said, Ferrari does offer an optional passenger display, which seems a little odd in a car like this. Maybe your nephew can watch Shrek while you lap COTA. The world is your oyster.
As you'd expect, Ferrari doesn't list prices for any of these options in its configurator. You'll have to contact your local dealer to find out how much any of them will set you back.
But getting into a new 296 Challenge Stradale will cost you at least $307,000 to start. And that's before you start checking boxes.

articles.title_orig: Marco Rubio’s concern about Jensen Huang, Nvidia being ‘malign influence’ led to Trump warning
articles.title_zh: Marco Rubio’s concern about Jensen Huang, Nvidia being ‘malign influence’ led to Trump warning
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Secretary of State Marco Rubio believed Jensen Huang and Nvidia were having a “malign influence” on US foreign policy toward China, prompting him to warn President Trump of the national security threats posed by the company, sources and officials told The Post.
Rubio’s “hawkish” stance predated revelations of Huang’s extramarital affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a suspected Chinese spy and former CEO of Megaspeed — a client of Nvidia’s that’s now accused of smuggling some of the firm’s most advanced AI chips into China.
“Rubio was solely concerned with the national security risks,” a US official told The Post, “and [Commerce Secretary Howard] Lutnick did not want to handcuff Nvidia in any way.”
“It was the president’s call,” the official said, referring to Trump pressuring Nvidia’s board into reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO this week.
A source close to the White House added that Rubio has a “personal dislike” of Huang.
Alice Huang’s Singapore-based AI and cloud computing firm was only blacklisted from trading with the US by the Commerce Department on Monday, months after Rubio first made his concerns known to the president in a May 2026 briefing on Air Force One en route to China.
Nvidia didn’t put its client Megaspeed on its “no sell” list until June 2025 — the same month that federal investigators sought an interview with Alice Huang.
“Marco views this as an arms-control-type issue, JD views this as an AI leadership issue,” one source close to the White House said.
A second source familiar with Jensen Huang’s comeback also cited Vance’s concern about AI.
“The President and VP became convinced that Jensen was a singular figure protecting Open Source models and preventing the closed-source model companies from becoming too powerful,” this person said.
A memo, overseen by Rubio and circulated to some Cabinet officials in March, warned that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang had connections to the Chinese government — but stopped short of saying she was a honeypot dispatched by Beijing to collect intel on Jensen Huang, according to one administration official.
The memo hadn’t definitively stated she was a Chinese spy tasked with collecting intelligence on Jensen Huang, nor was the Nvidia CEO ever given a defensive briefing on the Megaspeed exec by US intelligence, the official said.
Instead, the document contained some of the “circumstantial” ties to China’s Ministry of State Security, the official added, but others in the administration indicated that its contents didn’t alarm Trump — or alter his warm view of Jensen Huang.
A third administration official noted that Attorney General Todd Blanche also briefed Trump and Vance last weekend that the recently ousted Nvidia CEO presented no risk to national security — despite his dalliance with Alice Huang.
“Ultimately, POTUS sided with JD,” the source close to the White House added.
The New York Times, which first reported on Rubio’s memo, indicated that it was based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, who was in contact with Chinese intelligence while Jensen Huang was having an affair with her.
The substance of the Huang-Huang memo was drawn from a report authored by the CIA, according to The Washington Post .
The president cautioned in a Truth Social post Monday that Nvidia should still complete an internal investigation into Jensen Huang, even after his sudden return to the company.
“NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security,” Trump wrote in the post.
The DOJ is also still investigating Megaspeed for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
The president took questions on Friday flanked by Vance and Rubio, saying that Jensen Huang should also be given a “second chance” after confessing to the affair in order to resume his role at Nvidia.
Reports of the fling — as well as affairs with at least two other Nvidia employees — prompted Jensen Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12, even as Trump, Vance and Wall Streeters successfully lobbied for his return.
Three days later, the company’s board unanimously affirmed that.
The company saw its market cap rebound by $1 trillion , following mass sell-offs of stock last Friday.
“Trump was worried about the market sell-off last week and we could have gone into a recession overnight because so much of the country’s wealth is tied up in the AI trade and the data center build-out, which looked like it was faltering,” one corporate executive told The Post’s Charles Gasparino .
Reps for Nvidia, the White House, State Department, and CIA didn’t respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.title_zh: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office is expected to release the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to the people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
They stressed the timing for the rollout of the tariffs could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.
Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year that were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
The tariffs are in response to what the White House has said is excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has led to a flood of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies.
The anticipated action constitutes a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025 that the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. The White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10% to 12.5% in July, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
The anticipated trade action demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated. At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump.
Even with majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.

articles.title_orig: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed.
Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza reported on Monday that by the end of September, 490,000 Russian troops had been confirmed dead by Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat.
But accounting for time lags in reporting and including troops who have been reported as missing in action – and are most likely dead – Russian fatalities jump to more than 720,000 since the start of the war, according to the two outlets.
That is a staggering number that surpasses Russia’s death toll from the Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s and both Chechen wars in the 1990s and early 2000s – and which the Kremlin has long tried to keep secret.
The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe and there are two reasons it will get worse
Rosstat stopped publishing demographic data in 2025 to disguise the rising death toll from the war. Mediazona and Meduza, as well as other outlets, obtained the official data after two pro-Ukrainian hacker groups, Cyber ​​Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, managed to breach Rosstat’s servers earlier this month.
CNN cannot independently verify the figures, but the leaked data on confirmed deaths alone corroborates earlier estimates by analysts and Western intelligence – which now appear to fall far short of the likely real death toll.
Mediazona and Meduza have long been keeping a tally of Russian losses, based mostly on inheritance documents, death notices and other publicly available documents.
But the leaked Rosstat data allowed the media outlets to go a step further, using the same methods and calculations normally employed by actuaries estimating risks and insurance premiums.
By analyzing discrepancies between reported death dates and death registration dates, and by comparing these to search notices published by relatives, the reporters were able to extrapolate the number of deaths that have occurred but have not yet been reported to be somewhere around 230,000.
Mediazona has kept a tally of troops identified as missing by their relatives from 2023. That database contains 160,000 individuals and almost all of them are likely dead. Mediazona said that based on its reporting, the rate of survival among those reported missing only around 10%.
The data shared by Silent Crow showed that the war was the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion, after heart diseases; Covid; and stroke and other vascular conditions. It also confirms what has long been suspected – that the losses are not spread evenly across Russia, with poorer areas and ethnic minorities suffering significantly higher casualty rates.
In addition, an analysis by the NEST Centre, a think tank that also obtained the data, revealed the scale of Russia’s recruitment of foreign fighters. It identified 6,947 records of foreign nationals killed in Ukraine – the majority of them from the central Asian countries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
Like Russia, Ukraine doesn’t release official casualty data, although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly acknowledged the scale of losses in combat. The most recent research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July that the country has endured between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities.
Alexander Baunov, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said that the combined death toll suffered by Russia and Ukraine could exceed 1 million.
As the newly projected death toll underscores the human cost of Moscow’s war, fears are growing in Ukraine over a deteriorating security situation in the country’s eastern Donetsk region – an area mostly under Russian control – amid daily guided bomb and drone attacks .
All families with children still in Donetsk were on Tuesday ordered to evacuate.
Children and families in many communities in most of Ukrainian-controlled Donetsk - including the major cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk - were already under the evacuation order, but now the measure has been expanded to settlements further west. An estimated 64,500 civilians remain in the region as of November 2026, according to the Donetsk regional military administration.
“This is an extremely difficult but necessary decision. The Russians are shelling our cities and villages every day and bombarding the region with aerial bombs,” said the head of Donetsk’s regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin.
For months, Moscow’s forces have been inching towards Kramatorsk , one of Ukraine’s last strongholds in the north of Donetsk region. Tuesday’s mandatory evacuation order is a sign of Kyiv’s concern that an expansion of Russian attacks could further harm civilians and isolate communities, for example by blowing up bridges and supply routes.
CNN’s Clare Sebastian, Nathan Hodge, Kosta Gak and Lauren Kent contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia board joins Jensen Huang under scrutiny after reinstating embattled CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board joins Jensen Huang under scrutiny after reinstating embattled CEO
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s Truth Social account is many things: a disturbing stream of consciousness, a nationwide embarrassment, a place where professionalism and discretion (and truth) generally go to die. But, often, the feed is a gallery of self-portraits, many of which have been A.I.-generated. Trump as a pontiff; Trump as a king; Trump as a king and a fighter pilot, dumping sewage on protesters, in a video set to “Danger Zone,” by Kenny Loggins. In this context, the image that Trump posted on Monday —of a blood-splattered Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s newly reinstated C.E.O., victoriously hoisting a brassiere—might barely even register. And yet the photo is an anomaly, not because it’s so vulgar (this is the same account, after all, that once shared a clip of the Obamas as apes) but because it is glorifying someone who is not Donald Trump. If anything, the photo—a play on that photo , the iconic picture taken of Trump after he was nearly assassinated at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania—is a strange self-own, a diminishment of the event that helped Trump reclaim the Presidency, and a reminder of whose interests it is that the White House now serves.
The Lede Reporting and commentary on what you need to know today.
In the picture, which appears to be made with A.I., and posted, without a caption, Trump has been replaced by Huang, and the American flag by a black-and-green Nvidia flag. Huang is raising his fist, just as Trump did, but his fingers are clasped around a red underwire bra—red because bras are seemingly always red in the male imagination but also presumably because Huang’s initial downfall was prompted by allegations that he was sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy. As in the original shot, the man at the center of the picture is still flanked by Secret Service agents, a detail that feels like a lazy holdover; a cleverer meme might have swapped out the agents for Elon Musk and David Sacks, two of Huang’s most high-profile supporters. But perhaps the image of federal protection is apt. Not long after Nvidia announced Huang’s return—an about-face that came just eleven days after his resignation—Trump took credit for the company’s decision to bring Huang back. “I convinced them,” he told CNBC, in a hallucinatory, nearly hour-long phone interview. “I made the deal.” He noted, “We have to protect our geniuses, and he’s certainly a genius.”
It is ironic, to say the least, that one of the most anti-science Presidents in recent memory—one who has gutted university funding ; waged war against individual scientists, such as Anthony Fauci; and tried to make it much harder , through visa fees and restrictions, for immigrant scientists to study and work in America—is now claiming that he wants to protect geniuses. But it is true that Trump has consistently worked to protect Jensen Huang. On November 8th, Nvidia, the world’s biggest chip company, announced that it was opening an investigation into Huang, who had been romantically involved with a woman determined by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. (China has denied that the woman, Alice Huang, is a spy, but the Times recently reported that she “kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year,” during her relationship with the Nvidia C.E.O.) Trump was quick to describe Huang as “an honorable guy” who “probably has an excuse for it.” After talking to Huang, Trump explained, “He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him.” (Never mind that, this past May, the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, reportedly warned Trump about Alice Huang.)
Trump urged Huang not to step down from his role at Nvidia, but when Huang stepped down anyway, on November 12th—following reports of two more alleged extramarital affairs with non-spies, both of whom worked under him at Nvidia—Trump briefly pivoted to championing another genius. He suggested that the former Apple C.E.O. Tim Cook, a man whom Trump once referred to as “Tim Apple,” take Huang’s place. (“A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote, on Truth Social.) Unfortunately, the markets weren’t as optimistic about Nvidia’s future; the company’s stock price dropped more than sixteen per cent. Suddenly, Trump was on Fox News, saying that “we have to take care of our geniuses,” because “we don’t have that many of them.” On Monday, CNBC asked Trump whether the stock-market losses had prompted his intervention on behalf of Huang. Trump replied, “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me.”
In any case, after Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang, citing “input from senior levels of the United States government” in its announcement, the company’s shares surged more than thirty per cent. “The response from the market has been very positive,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal on Monday evening. “That really shows the decision was right.”
Trump’s obsession with the stock market isn’t new, although it has likely been amplified by recent events. The President, reeling from his party’s sweeping defeat in the midterm elections —a nationwide repudiation of his Administration’s policies and priorities, which have exacerbated the affordability crisis across the country—appears determined to avoid a stock-market collapse and an A.I.-bubble burst, outcomes that would further tank his standing in the final years of his Presidency. Perhaps even more significant are Trump’s personal financial ties with Nvidia. A Washington Post investigation found that the President’s holdings in the company ballooned to as much as sixty-two million dollars’ worth of stock before Huang’s scandals became public, with the value of those holdings appreciating amid a series of policy decisions and relaxing of restrictions that benefitted Nvidia’s bottom line. Huang has seemingly become one of Trump’s closest corporate allies not through a mutual quest to enhance American infrastructure, or to improve the country’s economic condition, but through their overlapping personal and financial interests. Genius recognizes genius.
Still, one assumes—or hopes—that Trump would be at least marginally alarmed by Huang’s entanglements with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. This is a President who, during his first term, instigated a trade war with China, persistently portraying Xi Jinping’s government as ruthlessly hostile to the U.S., and used a similar justification for implementing further tariffs on the country during his second term. Alice Huang isn’t just thought to have been a spy for the Chinese government; during her relationship with Jensen Huang, she also worked for the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia chips, which is alleged to have helped Chinese customers circumvent U.S. export controls. Last year, Trump told “60 Minutes” that no country “other than the United States” would have access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Megaspeed is the subject of a U.S. Justice Department probe into whether it facilitated the flow of advanced chips to China. (Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.)
In recent months, however, we’ve seen Trump’s antagonistic posture toward China soften. He’s been bragging about his “outstanding” relationship with Xi, and dismissing concerns about Chinese espionage and possible national-security threats. “Somebody said, ‘Oh, they spy on us,’ ” Trump recalled during a September exchange with reporters in the Oval Office. “And I said, ‘Maybe they do, but we spy on them, too.’ ” Trump took a similar tack in his CNBC interview on Monday, arguing that it didn’t matter if Alice Huang was in touch with China’s Ministry of State Security, since Trump himself was in contact with the agency, too. articles.title_orig: Jim Cramer sizes up six retail stocks after earnings — and names his two favorites
articles.title_zh: Jim Cramer sizes up six retail stocks after earnings — and names his two favorites
articles.content_orig:
CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday assessed the latest earnings reports from six major retailers, identifying which stocks have more room to run.
Retail stocks have been a bright spot the last few months as investors rotated out of technology stocks and oil prices and interest rates retreated from their highs. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT) has gained 9% this quarter, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) has plunged nearly 20% and the S&P 500 has shed almost 6%.
"Retailer earnings went great today, with all six major retailers that I was watching gaining ground, and several — including Dollar Tree, Dick's, Kohl's and Abercrombie & Fitch — notching strong double-digit gains," the " Mad Money " host said.
"That said, some reports were better than others," he added. "Burlington Stores and Kohl's basically just beat low expectations, Dick's had a nice bounce-back quarter, and Dollar Tree was very solid. But Best Buy and Abercrombie & Fitch, two of our favorite names in the group, had the best reports of all."
Here's where Cramer stands on each retailer.
Dollar Tree shares surged 11% after the discount retailer beat expectations for comparable sales, revenue and adjusted earnings per share and raised its full-year outlook. "This is a company that's been focused on self-help initiatives recently, and the combination of their progress on that front and the value proposition they can offer ... are driving the strong performance that we've seen from Dollar Tree recently," he said.
Burlington Stores missed comparable sales and revenue expectations while merely matching earnings estimates. Cramer attributed Tuesday's 4% rally to low expectations following a more than 30% decline from its all-time closing high on July 30, as well as the company's largely unchanged fourth-quarter outlook. He still prefers TJX Companies , which delivered a much stronger report last week , and is a holding in Cramer's Charitable Trust .
Dick's Sporting Goods shares jumped almost 15% after the retailer beat on top and bottom lines and raised its full-year earnings outlook. Despite inventory challenges across the athletic footwear and apparel industry, Cramer said Dick's is "controlling what it can control, taking market share while the market is muted, and setting itself up for long-term success."
Best Buy delivered "arguably the best set of numbers from any retailer that reported" despite posting the smallest stock gain of just 3%, Cramer said. Comparable sales rose more than 6%, and the electronics retailer also raised its full-year outlook, projecting comparable sales growth of 2% to 4% for the holiday quarter.
Cramer attributed the muted stock reaction to Best Buy's nearly 80% rally from its 52-week closing low on May 13. "At less than 15 times earnings, with a 3.9% yield and this latest quarter nearly for free, I think Best Buy is still a buy," he said.
Kohl's shares climbed 19% after the department store chain beat comparable sales and earnings expectations, though tariff refunds contributed significantly to the bottom-line beat. Like Burlington, Kohl's benefited from low expectations.
"Kohl's is a funky story," he said. "Credit to them for not doing as badly as the analysts expected them to. But it's still not a business that I'm a long-term believer in."
Abercrombie & Fitch shares surged almost 20% after the apparel retailer topped expectations and raised its full-year outlook. Cramer praised the company's disciplined inventory management, which has supported pricing power and margins.
"ANF can be a boom or bust stock, but right now it's booming, and I don't think it's done going higher," Cramer said.

articles.title_orig: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.title_zh: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.content_orig:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.

A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."

When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
