articles.title_orig: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.title_zh: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.content_orig:
Denmark's Supreme Court upheld on Monday a controversial law intended to eliminate ethnic enclaves in public housing, or "ghettos," as the government calls them, by giving authorities the ability to limit the number of "non-Western" immigrants and their descendants who can live in any particular housing development.
The court ruled that the eviction in 2022 of residents from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej, a housing development in the city of Helsingør, north of Copenhagen, did not constitute ethnic discrimination.
The Danish law introduced in 2018 is among Europe's most aggressive attempts to force immigrant communities to assimilate and to avoid the evolution of "parallel societies" in the country. It has attracted both international condemnation and admiration from politicians in other countries that seek to emulate Denmark's approach to immigration and integration.
Under the legislation, residential areas with at least 1,000 inhabitants, where more than 50% of residents are immigrants or descendants of immigrants from "non-Western" countries, and which meet certain socioeconomic criteria relating to employment rates, income levels, education attainment, and crime, can be subject to redevelopment requirements.
Housing developments designated as "transformation areas" are required to reduce the proportion of public family housing to no more than 40% by 2030. This can involve demolishing buildings, selling properties to private landlords, or converting them to other forms of housing, resulting in the eviction and relocation of some residents.
Under the law, non-Western countries include all nations outside the European Union, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Vatican State, the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand. The classification is based on a person's country of origin rather than their citizenship, which means even Danish citizens born and raised in Denmark can be classified as non-Western if both of their parents immigrated from non-Western countries.
The seven families evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej argued in their case that the distinction between Western and non-Western origins was effectively a proxy for ethnicity, and thus amounts to illegal discrimination based on race. The Supreme Court concluded that the distinction was based on nationality and country of birth rather than ethnicity, however, noting that both categories encompassed a wide range of ethnic groups and that people of the same ethnicity could fall into either category.
The court's ruling followed a decision last December by the European Union's highest court, which found that the Danish legislation could constitute discrimination on the grounds of ethnic origin, but the EU court left it to Denmark's courts to make the final determination.
Anders Svendsen, Chief Legal Officer for Denmark's national tenants' organization, LLO, told CBS News the organization didn't expect the Supreme Court to rule the way it did.
"We were slightly surprised, considering what the EU court had come up with previously last December," he said.
The organization estimates that several thousand homes have been demolished under the legislation already.
"A lot of people are still quite concerned, because they don't know if they're going to be next," Svendsen said. "This regulation has been quite unpopular among the renters in the public sector, but it has been quite popular in the population at large."
The LLO said it recognized the government's desire to promote social cohesion, but it questioned whether demolishing homes and reducing the availability of affordable housing was a proportionate response.
"We disagree, because it sees public housing as a problem to be solved and less public housing is seen as the cure," Svendsen told CBS News.
Joachim B. Olsen, a former Danish lawmaker who is now the opinion editor for the Danish newspaper B.T., was not surprised by Monday's ruling.
"Legislation is thoroughly vetted by the Department of Justice to make sure that it is in accordance with the constitution and Denmark's international obligations before it is presented to parliament," he told CBS News.
Olsen rejected the suggestion that the distinction between Western and non-Western origin was a proxy for race, arguing that it was based on cultural background.
"It is important to understand that the provisions in the 'ghetto law' apply to anyone living in the area designated as a 'ghetto,' no matter ethnicity or citizenship," he said.
Olsen argued that the policy had been broadly successful. According to Danish government figures , the number of neighborhoods officially classified as ghettos fell from 29 in 2018, to five in 2025.
"Incomes in these areas have risen. Employment is up. So is the educational level," he said. "Overall, I would say that positives outnumber the negatives."
Denmark has become a model for some other European governments as they look at ways to tighten immigration restrictions and address public concerns over the integration of immigrant communities.
While demands for tougher immigration policy in many European nations have been driven predominantly by right-wing populist parties, Denmark's restrictive approach has been championed by its center-left Social Democratic Party, led by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Frederiksen has been outspoken about her desire to preserve Danish culture and her opposition to a concept of multiculturalism in which all cultures are afforded equal standing in the country.
"We are a Danish society, and we form an ethnically Danish indigenous tribe," Frederiksen said last week on the B.T. newspaper's podcast, Borgerlig Tabloid . "Of course, this evolves when new people arrive here. But it is also necessary that, in the future, Denmark still has a strong majority culture."
Britain's government cited Denmark's policies earlier this year as it changed its own rules on people granted asylum in the U.K.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, announcing a new policy in March under which people granted asylum will have that status subject to regular review, said the "reset in Britain's asylum offer" had been "inspired by Denmark's success."
Denmark has also been at the forefront of efforts to establish "return hubs" — deportation centers outside Europe.
Last week, Denmark joined Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands in announcing plans to establish a "return hub" in Rwanda for migrants who have exhausted their legal avenues to remain in Europe, but who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

articles.title_zh: AG Blanche, FBI’s Patel dodge questions about Jensen Huang investigation
articles.content_orig:
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.content_orig:
The U.S. trade representative's office is set to unveil its latest tariff plans Tuesday night.
The Trump administration will propose new tariff hikes Tuesday night on the European Union, China, Mexico, Japan and 12 other trading partners, a major step towards recreating the president’s global duties the Supreme Court struck down in February.
According to one person with knowledge of the planning, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will announce the new tariff proposals as part of a report into the countries’ excess manufacturing capacity. The findings are the product of a trade investigation Greer’s office launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the U.S. trade representative to impose tariffs in response to unfair trade practices.
Three other people briefed by the administration on the investigation confirmed the report was in the process of being finalized and the results would be announced as soon as today. They were granted anonymity to share details of policy plans that are not yet public.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the announcement was coming.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.title_zh: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.content_orig:
His accounts continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, according to filings.
President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.
His accounts have continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, including more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of Nvidia stock this year through September, according to separate filings that disclose trades in his accounts.
The White House continues to maintain that third-party institutions manage Trump's accounts.
"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle.
"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."
Trump has repeatedly vouched for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the scandal surrounding his alleged afair with a woman U.S. intelligence alleges is a Chinese asset.
On Monday, he took credit for Huang's stunning return to Nvidia , saying in an interview that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back as CEO.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump, who had urged Huang's reinstatement publicly, said in a phone interview with CNBC .
Following the announcement, the major stock indexes rebounded sharply on Monday as Nvidia shares closed up more than 30%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,447.98 points, or 3.0%, while the S & P 500 jumped over 4.73%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq soared over 6.5%.
Shares of Nvidia surged, recovering nearly all of the losses suffered since Nov. 12, the day Nvidia announced Huang's resignation .
Nvidia develops the semiconductor chips, systems, and software powering artificial intelligence. In early October 2026, its market valuation reached $5.8 trillion.
Given its significant presence in the stock market, Nvidia is a common holding in many investment portfolios and Trump's shares in the company represent a small portion of his overall portfolio.

articles.title_orig: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.title_zh: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.content_orig:
Late last month, CF40 Research , the research arm of the China Finance 40 Forum-a leading non-governmental think tank specializing in economics, shared its annual flagship report, China’s Economy: Toward a New Paradigm—Drivers, Trends, and Policy Implications , at its 2026 Bund Summit .
Guo Kai , President of CF40 Research and a former Chinese central bank official, kindly shared a copy and allowed me to share an excerpt.
The following passages are from the report’s English text. They have been rearranged and intervening material omitted; section headings and this introduction are mine. Corporate debt and profit figures below refer to its sample of A-share-listed companies outside finance and petroleum.
By 2026, the current real estate adjustment may not yet have fully run its course, but signs of structural stabilization have begun to emerge. After five years of deep adjustment, housing sales, investment, inventories, and developers’ balance sheets have entered a new phase, while house-price declines have begun to moderate. Few would expect the real estate sector to return to its former “golden age,” but the drag from the ongoing adjustment on the economy has diminished markedly at the margin. In other words, real estate is gradually shifting from the economy’s largest source of downward pressure toward a more stable influence.
Based on our analysis of international real estate corrections, China’s current real estate adjustment has already been considerable in both duration and magnitude, and the market has likely entered a bottoming phase. Further adjustment remains possible, but another sharp contraction appears unlikely.
Since the start of 2026, China’s real estate market has begun to show signs of “structural stabilization.” We selected 33 core cities for analysis, including the four first-tier cities—Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen—and major second-tier cities such as Hangzhou, Suzhou, Qingdao, Wuhan, and Hefei. We find that house prices, the floor area of new homes sold, and existing-home transaction volumes have all shown signs of stabilizing in these cities. House prices have even risen modestly in a few core cities. By contrast, real estate markets in most third- and fourth-tier cities remain weak. In other words, stabilization is concentrated in core cities rather than broad-based, which is why we refer to it as “structural stabilization.”
Thus, for the 33 core cities, if new starts continue to decline sharply, excess housing inventory could be rapidly reduced, potentially giving way to a shortage. This would provide additional support for house prices and demand and could accelerate the housing market’s recovery.
Over the past few years, the deep adjustment in the real estate market has been the main driver of the widening current account surplus. The underlying mechanism is that the real estate downturn led to a sharp decline in the investment rate, while the saving rate adjusted with a lag. The resulting widening of the saving–investment gap translated directly into a larger current account surplus.
As the real estate market gradually stabilizes, the drag from real estate investment will diminish, while household precautionary saving will stop rising. The saving–investment gap will therefore narrow, and the current account surplus will stabilize at a high level rather than continue to widen. This process bears some resemblance to the decline in China’s current account surplus after 2008, when the RMB 4 trillion stimulus package drove a sharp expansion in domestic investment, significantly narrowing the saving–investment gap.
By contrast, the stabilization of the manufacturing capacity cycle since 2024 has clearly not relied on comparable demand-side stimulus. Instead, the sequence has been “supply adjustment first, followed by a moderate recovery in demand”: a market-driven process in which firms voluntarily slowed investment and retired inefficient capacity in response to weak demand. This differs fundamentally from the post-2016 cyclical reversal driven by a sharp rebound in demand.
According to CF40 research, the new economy’s total value added rose from about 6.1% of GDP in 2018 to 10.4% in 2025, while the corresponding share for real estate fell from 12.7% to 8.4%. By 2025, the new economy’s total value-added share had surpassed that of real estate and had become an important component of GDP.
A defining characteristic of new-economy firms is their greater emphasis on R&D and their ability to generate more operating revenue and profits with less debt. In 2025, new-economy firms accounted for only 11.9% of the total interest-bearing debt of firms in the full sample, compared with 17.8% of total operating revenue and 29.5% of total net profits across the sample. Their share of total R&D expenditure was even higher, at 47.6%. As the new economy accounts for a growing share of China’s economy, the country’s growth model will gradually evolve.
The negative wealth effect of the real estate adjustment is fading, but households’ propensity to consume remains well below its pre-pandemic level, while further improvements in social security and public services are constrained by fiscal pressures. Rather than rising sharply, the consumption rate is therefore more likely to stabilize as the drag from real estate fades. If supportive policies are fully implemented, the consumption rate could gradually rise.
Moreover, the more advanced a manufacturing industry, the lower the share of output going to compensation of employees tends to be. For example, compensation of employees accounts for only 7.8% and 7.6% of gross output in electrical machinery and equipment manufacturing and automobile manufacturing, respectively—two industries that together encompass the “new three.” The corresponding share is 8.7% in computer, communications, and other electronic equipment manufacturing, the industry most closely associated with AI.
On a value-added basis, compensation of employees accounts for 36%, 42%, and 47% in these three industries, respectively, all below the service-sector average. This means that even if the new economy continues to expand rapidly and drive economic growth, households’ share of income in primary distribution will not automatically increase and could even decline. This is because these new-economy industries allocate a smaller share of their output to compensation of employees than the current economy-wide average.
On monetary policy, emphasis should move further away from pursuing credit-volume expansion toward lowering interest rates, improving inflation expectations, and restoring nominal demand. Real estate no longer performs its previous role in credit expansion, while the new economy is relatively less dependent on bank credit. Growth in bank lending and total social financing is therefore increasingly difficult to use on its own as a measure of whether monetary policy is sufficiently accommodative.
One possible aggregate benchmark is that “nominal growth in broad fiscal expenditure should exceed nominal GDP growth.” At present, local governments face multiple constraints, including declining land-related revenues, debt resolution efforts, and rising mandatory spending commitments. Near-term fiscal expansion will therefore need to rely more heavily on the central government.
The new economy has demonstrated China’s capacity to create new productive capacity, but the more important issue for the next stage is how to translate that capacity into household income and final consumption. New-economy firms have high R&D spending, high productivity, and low reliance on debt—an important direction for economic transformation. However, if the industrial structure merely shifts from traditional manufacturing toward more advanced manufacturing, higher productivity will not necessarily translate automatically into a larger household income share or a higher consumption rate.
